content: Antimalarial drugs are specifically formulated to either prevent or treat malaria. Certain antimalarial agents, such as chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine, are also utilized in managing autoimmune conditions like rheumatoid arthritis and lupus-associated arthritis. Numerous antimalarial drugs are available on the market, with quinine being the oldest and most well-known. Quinine Quinine has a historical origin in Peru, where the bark of the Cinchona tree was discovered to have medicinal properties. It remains a widely used treatment for malaria, particularly in severe cases. Quinine is an alkaloid that functions as a blood schizonticidal agent and a weak gametocide, particularly effective against Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium malariae. It accumulates in the food vacuoles of Plasmodium species, especially Plasmodium falciparum, and inhibits hemozoin biocrystallization, leading to the accumulation of cytotoxic heme. Although less effective and more toxic than chloroquine, quinine is still highly effective in treating acute severe P. falciparum infections, especially in regions with high resistance to chloroquine, mefloquine, and sulfa drug-pyrimethamine combinations. It is also used for post-exposure treatment in individuals returning from malaria-endemic areas. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends a dosage of 8 mg/kg three times daily for 3–7 days, depending on parasite sensitivity and adherence levels. In areas with increased quinine resistance, it is combined with doxycycline, tetracycline, or clindamycin. Quinine can be administered orally, intravenously, or intramuscularly. However, its use is often associated with a syndrome called cinchonism, which includes symptoms such as tinnitus, rashes, vertigo, nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. Neurological effects, including confusion, delirium, and coma, may occur due to its neurotoxic properties. Quinine can also induce hypoglycemia by stimulating insulin secretion, necessitating regular glucose monitoring, especially in pregnant patients. Overdose or prolonged use can lead to renal failure and respiratory depression, potentially resulting in death. Other Alkaloids Quinimax and quinidine are two commonly used alkaloids related to quinine. Quinimax is a combination of four alkaloids (quinine, quinidine, cinchonine, and cinchonidine) and has shown greater efficacy than quinine due to synergistic effects. Quinidine, a stereoisomer of quinine, shares similar antimalarial properties and is reserved for severe malaria cases. Chloroquine Chloroquine was historically the most widely used antimalarial drug and served as the prototype for many subsequent treatments. It is cost-effective, well-tested, and safe, but its efficacy has declined due to the emergence of drug-resistant strains of Plasmodium. Despite this, it remains the first-line treatment in many sub-Saharan African countries. Chloroquine is a 4-aminoquinoline compound that raises the internal pH of the parasite's vacuoles, inhibiting hemozoin biocrystallization and poisoning the parasite with toxic heme. It also interferes with parasitic nucleic acid biosynthesis. Chloroquine is effective against all forms of schizonts (except chloroquine-resistant P. falciparum and P. vivax) and gametocytes of P. vivax, P. malariae, P. ovale, and immature P. falciparum gametocytes. It has antipyretic and anti-inflammatory effects, making it useful even in resistant cases. The recommended dosage is 25 mg/kg over 3 days, with a pharmacokinetically superior regimen involving an initial dose of 10 mg/kg followed by 5 mg/kg at 6–8-hour intervals. For chemoprophylaxis, 5 mg/kg weekly is advised. Chloroquine is considered safe during pregnancy but may cause intolerable itching. Amodiaquine Amodiaquine, structurally similar to chloroquine, is often used in combination with it but is also effective as monotherapy. It clears parasites more effectively in uncomplicated malaria, leading to faster recovery. However, fatal adverse effects noted in the 1980s reduced its use in chemoprophylaxis. The WHO recommends its use when the risk of untreated infection outweighs potential side effects. It is particularly effective and less toxic in HIV-positive patients. The dosage is 25–35 mg/kg over 3 days, with side effects similar to chloroquine, including bradycardia, itching, nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. Pyrimethamine Pyrimethamine is used for uncomplicated malaria, particularly chloroquine-resistant P. falciparum strains when combined with sulfadoxine. It inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, halting DNA synthesis, cell division, and reproduction. It primarily acts on schizonts during hepatic and erythrocytic phases. Sulfadoxine Sulfadoxine inhibits the synthesis of dihydropteroic acid by blocking the use of para-aminobenzoic acid. Combined with pyrimethamine, it prevents two key stages of DNA synthesis in Plasmodium. It is mainly used for P. falciparum infections but is less active against other strains. Its long half-life exerts selection pressure on parasites, encouraging resistance. Severe skin reactions limit its use in chemoprophylaxis. Proguanil Proguanil, a biguanide derivative of pyrimidine, is converted to its active metabolite cycloguanil, which inhibits malarial dihydrofolate reductase. It acts on primary tissue stages of P. falciparum, P. vivax, and P. ovale but has no effect on hypnozoites. It is used prophylactically in combination with chloroquine. The recommended dosage is 3 mg/kg daily, with minimal side effects such as hair loss and mouth ulcers. Mefloquine Mefloquine, developed during the Vietnam War, is chemically related to quinine and effective against multi-drug-resistant P. falciparum. It acts by forming toxic heme complexes that damage parasitic food vacuoles. It is used for prophylaxis and acute therapy of resistant strains, often in combination with artesunate. Side effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, dizziness, and neurological events such as anxiety, hallucinations, and psychosis. It is not recommended during the first trimester of pregnancy. Halofantrine Halofantrine, a phenanthrene methanol, is effective against all Plasmodium species but is rarely used due to high cost, variable bioavailability, and cardiotoxicity. It is reserved for severe, resistant malaria in patients without heart disease. The recommended dose is 8 mg/kg in three doses at six-hour intervals. Side effects include nausea, abdominal pain, and severe ventricular dysrhythmias. Primaquine Primaquine, an 8-aminoquinoline, is the only drug effective against hypnozoites, making it essential for curing relapsing malaria caused by P. vivax and P. ovale. It also acts on gametocytes and blood schizonts. The mechanism involves generating oxygen free radicals that disrupt the parasite's electron transport chain. The dosage for relapse prevention is 15 mg/kg for 14 days. Side effects include anorexia, nausea, vomiting, and anemia. Artemisinin and Derivatives Artemisinin, derived from the plant Artemisia annua, has been used for over 1,000 years in traditional Chinese medicine. It is effective against multi-drug-resistant P. falciparum and is always used in combination therapy to prevent resistance. Artemisinin acts rapidly, clearing parasites within 1–3 days, and inhibits the sarcoplasmic/endoplasmic reticulum calcium ATPase of P. falciparum. Side effects are minimal but may include headaches, nausea, and dark urine. Artemether: A methyl ether derivative with reduced hypnozoiticidal activity, used in combination therapy for severe cases. Artesunate: A hemisuccinate derivative, the most frequently used artemisinin drug, effective in uncomplicated P. falciparum. Dihydroartemisinin: The active metabolite of artemisinin, with strong schizonticidal action. Arteether: An ethyl ether derivative used in combination therapy for resistant P. falciparum. Other Agents Doxycycline: A tetracycline antibiotic used for chemoprophylaxis in quinine-resistant areas. It inhibits protein synthesis by binding to the 30S ribosomal subunit. Side effects include enamel hypoplasia, bone growth depression, and photosensitivity. Clindamycin: A lincosamide antibiotic used in combination with quinine for resistant P. falciparum. Side effects include nausea, vomiting, and pseudomembranous colitis. Drug Resistance Antimalarial resistance occurs when parasites survive despite adequate drug administration. Resistance is confirmed through in vivo, in vitro, and molecular techniques. Factors contributing to resistance include non-compliance, poor drug quality, and incorrect dosing. Resistance development varies among Plasmodium species.
